summary: RFC 8554 defines HSS/LMS hash-based signatures. This document adds parameter sets that use other hash functions, including ones that give notably smaller signatures while still expected to offer enough security.

plainLanguage.summary: A signature made with a long stamp takes lots of space. This adds shorter stamps that still look safe, so signed messages need less room.

subtitle: Smaller hash-based signatures using alternative hash functions.

tldr.problem: RFC 8554 defines HSS/LMS hash-based signatures, which are believed to have excellent security but produce large signatures (1 to 4 kilobytes). For resource-constrained systems, this size is a significant limitation.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC adds new parameter sets that use truncated or alternative hash functions (SHA-256/192, SHAKE256/256, SHAKE256/192) instead of full SHA-256, reducing signature sizes by 35-40% while maintaining adequate security.
tldr.outcome: Applications can now choose between smaller signatures with a reduced but still adequate security margin, or stick with the original larger signatures for maximum security. The RFC is an informational IRTF research result.

today: RFC 9858 is an Informational document from the IRTF Crypto Forum Research Group. It is not an Internet Standard and is intended to guide research and future standardization. The parameter sets have been included in NIST SP 800-208 and are available for implementers to use as they see fit.

sections.title: Hash-Based Signatures and Size Trade-Offs
sections.content:
RFC 8554 defines the Hierarchical Signature System with Leighton-Micali Signatures (HSS/LMS), a stateful hash-based digital signature method. Hash-based signatures use only basic cryptographic operations and are believed to remain secure even against quantum computers. However, they have a disadvantage: signatures are large, typically between 1 and 4 kilobytes.

This RFC extends HSS/LMS by defining new parameter sets that use alternative hash functions. These new sets significantly reduce signature size at the cost of accepting a somewhat lower security margin. The trade-off makes sense for applications where bandwidth, storage, or processing power are constrained.
sections.plainLanguage: A signature that proves you sent a message takes a lot of space. These new signatures are shorter but still trustworthy enough for most uses.

sections.title: The New Hash Functions
sections.content:
The RFC defines three new hash functions for use in HSS/LMS:

SHA-256/192 is SHA-256 truncated to 192 bits. It produces output 24 bytes instead of SHA-256's 32 bytes, using the same algorithm and initialization as standard SHA-256. The truncation is safe because each message hashed in HSS includes a random value and a unique identifier, so the truncated hash cannot be treated as a prefix of the full hash.

SHAKE256/256 and SHAKE256/192 are based on the extendable-output function SHAKE256. SHAKE256/256 takes the first 256 bits of SHAKE256 output, while SHAKE256/192 takes the first 192 bits. Both offer efficient hashing and allow for diversity in implementations. SHAKE256 was chosen over SHAKE128 because it has stronger preimage resistance, which is critical for hash-based signatures.

Using SHAKE-based functions alongside SHA-based ones increases cryptographic diversity. Implementations can choose whichever works better on their platform without sacrificing security.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of using the full-length stamp algorithm, these use shorter versions. Some cut a standard algorithm short; others use a different algorithm that works faster and makes shorter stamps.

sections.title: Parameter Sets for Signing
sections.content:
The RFC defines new parameter sets for both LM-OTS (one-time signatures) and LMS (many-time signatures). Each set specifies which hash function to use, the output size, and details like the Winternitz parameter w (which controls the number of chains in a signature) and Merkle tree height.

For LM-OTS, there are 12 new sets: four using SHA-256/192, four using SHAKE256/256, and four using SHAKE256/192. Each set varies w (1, 2, 4, or 8) to trade signature size for computation time.

For LMS, there are 15 new sets controlling Merkle tree height (the tree is used to sign multiple messages with one key). All of these parameter sets are assigned IANA-registered identifiers so that signatures include a code indicating which set was used.
sections.plainLanguage: A signature has different options: you can choose a faster way or a smaller stamp, and you pick which algorithm to use. The system remembers your choice so the other side knows how to check it.

sections.title: Size and Speed Trade-Offs
sections.content:
Switching from 256-bit hashes to 192-bit hashes affects three things: signature size, computation time, and security strength.

For signature size, using 192-bit hashes reduces it by 35 to 40% compared to 256-bit parameters. This comes from two effects: each hash in the signature is shorter (24 bytes instead of 32), and fewer Winternitz chains are needed because there is less data to encode.

For computation time, the first effect is irrelevant (the hash computation itself does not get faster), but the second still applies. For example, with Winternitz parameter w=8, SHA-256-based signatures need 34 chains but SHA-256/192 needs only 26 chains. Since the majority of time is spent computing Winternitz chains, this reduction gives real performance gains of roughly 20%.

In contrast, SHAKE256/256 offers no size or speed advantage over SHA-256, since both use 256-bit hashes. Its purpose is to provide an alternative for diversity or platform-specific performance reasons.
sections.plainLanguage: A shorter stamp takes less space and is a bit faster to make. A different algorithm might run faster on your computer, even if the stamp is the same size.

sections.title: Security Strength and Quantum Resistance
sections.content:
The security of these schemes rests on the difficulty of finding preimages in the hash functions. Using the analysis in academic cryptography, the security level of SHAKE256/256 is equivalent to 256-bit symmetric encryption (like AES-256), while SHA-256/192 and SHAKE256/192 offer security equivalent to 192-bit encryption (like AES-192). If these symmetric algorithms resist quantum computers, so should the hash-based signatures.

For classical computers, no attack is known better than trying about 2^192 hash computations for the 192-bit versions, which is infeasible in practice. For quantum computers, Grover's algorithm in theory could reduce this, but running billions of Grover algorithm instances in parallel over many quantum computers for years makes even that attack impractical.

One corner case occurs in schemes where the signer must be prevented from generating the same signature for two different messages. Since HSS uses randomization, this is normally infeasible, but the security margin is somewhat lower (128 bits for SHAKE256/256 and 96 bits for the 192-bit versions) if that assumption is needed. This remains well above the security requirements for most applications.
sections.plainLanguage: Breaking these would take more computing power than exists on Earth. Even a quantum computer would need to run for years with unimaginably many copies of itself.
